Modern web and cloud application architectures depend heavily on Representational State Transfer (REST) APIs as the primary communication backbone connecting distributed microservices, web clients, and mobile applications. However, this decentralization expands the attack surface, making authorization vulnerabilities—specifically Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA, OWASP API1:2023) and Broken Function Level Authorization (BFLA, OWASP API5:2023)—the most pervasive and critical threats in contemporary software engineering. Unlike syntactic injection flaws, authorization vulnerabilities typically return valid HTTP 200 responses containing well-formed business objects, rendering conventional Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools and single-request Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) utilities ineffective. Existing dynamic tools suffer from false-positive rates ranging from 40% to 60%, encounter persistent 404 Not Found dead-ends when querying dependent endpoints with uninstantiated resource IDs, execute third-party fuzzers without container isolation, and terminate at detection without automated developer remediation.

To bridge this critical gap, this project develops OFFAT-X, an advanced, sandboxed, dependency-aware, and role-differential framework for automated REST API authorization testing. OFFAT-X parses OpenAPI specifications to synthesize a directed producer-consumer dependency graph G = (V, E), dynamically traverses resource creation paths using Breadth-First Search (BFS) with depth bounded to L ≤ 4 steps, and eliminates 404 setup dead-ends. The framework evaluates authorization boundaries across a four-tier role-differential matrix (Guest < Low < Premium < Admin), combining horizontal cross-tenant replays with vertical privilege escalations. To safely discover undocumented routes and shadow APIs (OWASP API9:2023), OFFAT-X runs dictionary path brute-forcing inside hardened ephemeral Docker containers with dropped Linux capabilities (CAP_DROP ALL), no-new-privileges flags, and read-only root filesystems. False alarms are systematically eliminated via a mathematical Semantic Response Diffing Engine that evaluates Jaccard schema similarity, victim identifier overlap, HTTP status codes, and error signature penalties.

Crucially, OFFAT-X closes the feedback loop between vulnerability detection and developer remediation through automated OASIS SARIF 2.1.0 reporting and a composite GitHub Action that gates pull-request merges on newly introduced Critical and High severity findings. Across extensive empirical evaluations conducted on standardized benchmark targets (OWASP crAPI, VAmPI, OWASP Juice Shop, and an In-House Multi-Role API), OFFAT-X achieved an overall Precision of 0.941, Recall of 0.912, F1-Score of 0.926, and an ultra-low False Positive Rate of just 4.15%, representing an 89.9% reduction in false alarms compared to baseline OpenAPI scanners. The platform exhibited predictable bounded execution overhead (≤ 28 requests per target), sustained high reconnaissance throughput (50 req/sec), and verified complete containment across all test suites, establishing an autonomous, enterprise-grade DevSecOps security pipeline.

Software security has emerged as one of the most critical engineering disciplines in contemporary computer science. Modern web and cloud applications are developed at unprecedented velocities, driven by continuous integration and automated deployment pipelines that release new code to production dozens of times each day. In the modern cloud ecosystem, Representational State Transfer (REST) APIs serve as the foundational nervous system connecting mobile clients, single-page web frontends, and distributed microservices. However, this architectural decentralization profoundly expands the attack surface, creating systemic authorization fragility across modern enterprise platforms.

The practical difficulty in modern DevSecOps is therefore one of human attention, fragmented context, and alert fatigue, rather than a lack of scanning tools. Authorization failures—specifically Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA, CWE-639) and Broken Function Level Authorization (BFLA, CWE-285)—rank first and fifth in the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023). Unlike syntactic injection flaws, authorization weaknesses produce valid HTTP 200 responses containing well-formed business objects. Consequently, traditional static scanners (SAST) and single-request dynamic scanners (DAST) suffer from notorious false-positive rates of 40% to 60%, while remaining blind to relational multi-identity authorization breaches.

Earlier generations of vulnerability scanners leaned heavily on rigid syntactic patterns, which are fast but tend to flood a team with findings that are not actually exploitable in runtime contexts. OWASP OFFAT provides an open baseline for specification-driven testing, but its documented checks execute in complete isolation without stateful resource creation, trust status codes blindly, run without container sandboxing, and lack automated pull-request remediation. This leaves overworked engineering teams with the arduous burden of manual triage and patch drafting.

Recent breakthroughs in API testing frameworks demonstrate that authorization flaws can be reliably uncovered only by comparing multiple authenticated identities across stateful resource lifecycles. However, automating this process surfaces three severe engineering challenges: (i) resolving producer-consumer dependencies to avoid 404 setup dead-ends, (ii) differentiating normal 200 OK error envelopes from genuine data exfiltration, and (iii) containing third-party reconnaissance utilities to prevent testing host compromise.

Building a unified scanning platform surfaces three practical engineering challenges that do not show up in narrow tools. First, stateful dependency chaining must be bounded to prevent combinatorial request explosion. Second, multi-role matrix testing requires strict isolation between horizontal tenant accounts (Alice vs Bob) and vertical privilege tiers (Guest < Low < Premium < Admin). Third, third-party brute-force reconnaissance (such as DIRB) must execute within hardened, ephemeral sandboxes to prevent container escapes or unauthorized scanning.

OFFAT-X addresses these fundamental challenges by combining stateful dependency-aware chaining, a four-tier role-differential matrix, an ephemeral Docker sandbox, a mathematical semantic response diffing engine, and automated CI/CD merge gating into a unified platform. Built from the ground up to shorten the distance between finding a vulnerability and merging a verified fix, OFFAT-X parses OpenAPI specifications, synthesizes a directed dependency graph G=(V,E), executes setup calls using bounded BFS (L ≤ 4), and flags True Vulnerabilities via Equation (2) (D ≥ τ = 0.70).

A hallmark innovation of OFFAT-X is automated remediation. Every identified vulnerability is triaged using CVSS v3.1 scoring, mapped to official OWASP API Top 10 categories and MITRE CWEs, and paired with context-aware source code remediation directives (such as tenant ownership filters in Prisma/SQL and RBAC route middleware in Express). The findings are exported as standardized OASIS SARIF 2.1.0 reports, enabling direct integration with GitHub Advanced Security.

Around the clock, an autonomous GitHub Actions merge gate tracks pull requests touching OpenAPI specifications. The security gate evaluates test findings against the default branch baseline using structural endpoint fingerprints, blocking merges only on new Critical or High severity findings. This ensures zero alert fatigue while guaranteeing that unauthorized privilege escalation paths cannot be merged into production branches.

The scope of this project is stated deliberately: OFFAT-X is an automated authorization testing and DevSecOps verification platform for REST APIs. It establishes a sandboxed, dependency-aware testing pipeline that delivers verified exploit evidence, near-zero false alarms (4.2% FPR), and actionable developer remediation.

The remainder of this report is organised as follows. Chapter 2 reviews prior work on API security testing, grammar fuzzing, and container sandboxing. Chapter 3 presents the system analysis, comparing existing tools with OFFAT-X. Chapter 4 develops the materials, methodology, and mathematical formulation. Chapter 5 details the experimental setup across four benchmark targets. Chapter 6 provides exhaustive empirical results, confusion matrices, and ablation studies. Chapter 7 concludes the report and outlines future research.

Automated software security analysis sits at the intersection of static code analysis, dynamic application testing, specification-driven fuzzing, and container isolation. This chapter conducts a comprehensive survey of prior work, identifying foundational techniques and pinpointing the unresolved research gaps that motivated OFFAT-X.
2.1.1 Specification-Driven API Fuzzing and Grammar Analysis

The earliest generation of REST API fuzzers relied on unstructured parameter mutation, generating malformed strings that triggered trivial input validation errors rather than deep business logic bugs. Atlidakis et al. [3] introduced RESTler, the first stateful REST API fuzzer that analyzes OpenAPI specification contracts to dynamically infer producer-consumer dependencies among request operations. RESTler tracks resource creation responses and dynamically substitutes synthesized identifiers into subsequent consumer requests.

To overcome these limitations, the research community transitioned toward grammar-based and evolutionary testing. Arcuri [15] developed EvoMaster, applying evolutionary search algorithms to generate automated system test cases for web APIs. While EvoMaster demonstrated high branch coverage in white-box settings, it requires source-code bytecode instrumentation and lacks multi-identity authorization differential matrices.

In parallel, recent studies investigated grammar-driven sequence generation for microservices. However, stateful fuzzers remain predominantly crash-oriented: their objective functions maximize HTTP 500 errors and code coverage rather than detecting unauthorized HTTP 200 data leaks.

Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) inspects running applications from the outside in. PortSwigger [4] developed Autorize, a popular Burp Suite extension widely employed in manual web penetration testing. Autorize intercepts HTTP traffic generated by a human tester logged in as an administrative user and automatically replays each request using low-privileged session cookies.

While DAST tools and dual-identity extensions are inherently immune to source-code false positives—since they evaluate real HTTP responses from live deployments—they are fundamentally passive. Tools like Autorize [4] and Auto-IDOR-Hunter [5] require human testers to manually navigate application workflows, rendering them unscalable to hundreds of endpoints.

OWASP Foundation [2] established OWASP OFFAT as an open-source testing platform capable of translating OpenAPI specifications into automated security test cases. OFFAT checks for unrestricted HTTP verbs, parameter tampering, basic BOLA, and injection patterns.

However, baseline OFFAT executes all evaluations via single-request invocations. When evaluating endpoints requiring existing database entities, it transmits random identifiers, receives 404 Not Found, and records inconclusive results. Furthermore, OFFAT trusts status codes blindly, misclassifying 200 OK error envelopes as critical leaks.

The Dark Raver [10] developed DIRB, an established web content scanner that probes web servers using dictionary attack lists to discover hidden paths and files. When executing brute-force reconnaissance against staging or production environments, running untrusted fuzzing scripts directly on testing servers presents severe supply-chain and host compromise risks.

Simultaneously, container security research has advanced significantly. Docker Inc. [11] published formal container hardening guidelines establishing that dropping Linux capabilities (CAP_DROP ALL), applying no-new-privileges flags, mounting root filesystems as read-only, and utilizing temporary memory tmpfs structures provides robust containment against lateral network movement.

Taken together, the reviewed body of literature establishes that while each individual facet of application security testing has matured in isolation, the field remains critically fragmented. Fuzzers are stateful but crash-oriented; proxy extensions are authorization-aware but purely passive; baseline scanners are contract-driven but stateless and false-alarm prone; and reconnaissance scripts execute without security containment.

The research gap addressed by OFFAT-X follows directly from these findings. There exists an acute need for a unified framework that combines specification DAG parsing, stateful BFS chaining, a four-tier role-differential matrix, semantic response diffing, ephemeral container sandboxing, and automated PR merge gating.
Application security testing architectures in current commercial and open-source use fall predominantly into four isolated, uncoordinated operational categories.
The first category comprises standalone Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools (such as SonarQube, Semgrep, and ESLint-Security) that inspect source code files prior to deployment.
The second category comprises Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) scanners (such as OWASP ZAP and baseline OWASP OFFAT) that transmit external HTTP probes against live application endpoints.
The third category comprises ad-hoc manual penetration testing and standalone dictionary brute-force utilities (such as DIRB, Gobuster, and Autorize) used by specialized security consultants.
The fourth category comprises production availability and synthetic monitoring services that verify HTTP 200 availability after deployment.
The limitations of existing fragmented security systems are summarized below:
• Stateless 404 setup dead-ends: Single-request scanners query dependent endpoints with uninstantiated resource IDs, failing to evaluate BOLA authorization.
• Severe false-positive rates and alert fatigue: Conventional scanners trust status codes blindly, triggering false alarms whenever an error envelope returns 200 OK.
• Single-identity blind spots: Lacking multi-role privilege differential, existing tools cannot detect BFLA administrative privilege escalation.
• Unsandboxed reconnaissance risks: Executing third-party fuzzers directly on test runners exposes host environments to malicious payloads and lateral pivoting.
• Combinatorial request explosion: Naive multi-step sequence generators suffer state explosion, executing thousands of redundant requests.
• Lack of automated remediation: Existing scanners terminate at detection, leaving patch drafting and PR creation entirely to developers.
• Disconnected CI/CD gating: Vulnerability findings are trapped in PDF reports or terminal logs without automated SARIF merge gates.
• Combinatorial State Space Explosion in Stateful Workflows: Naive fuzzers experience exponential state explosion when attempting unguided multi-parameter permutations across deep API chains.
• Container Host Exposure in Automated Dynamic Scanners: Executing active path brute-forcing directly from host environments risks credential leakage and host network compromise.

Built to unify contract specifications with runtime authorization verification, OFFAT-X operates through an autonomous multi-tier architecture.

Processing within OFFAT-X is orchestrated across six modular layers: Specification & DAG Ingestion, Stateful Chaining Planner, Four-Tier Role-Differential Matrix, Ephemeral Sandboxed Reconnaissance, Semantic Response Diffing Engine, and DevSecOps CI/CD Integration.
The operational merits of the proposed OFFAT-X framework are summarized below:
• Zero 404 setup dead-ends: Autonomous BFS chaining provisions prerequisite resource entities prior to testing consumer routes.
• Drastic false positive reduction (4.2% FPR): Semantic diffing evaluates schema similarity, value overlap, and error signatures via Equation (2).

Figure 4.1 depicts the sequential eight-stage scanning and analysis pipeline implemented in OFFAT-X. The subsequent subsections develop the mathematical formulation, algorithmic mechanics, and operational controls of each pipeline phase.
Fig no: 4.1 End-to-End OFFAT-X Methodology Pipeline Flowchart Diagram

Before any tests are generated, specification ingestion normalizes OpenAPI 2.0 and 3.x specifications into a standardized schema representation. Let O = {o_1, o_2, ..., o_n} denote the set of API operations defined in the contract. A Directed Acyclic Graph G = (V, E) is synthesized where vertices V = O represent endpoints and directed edges e = (p, c) ∈ E represent producer-consumer relationships.

An operation p is designated a producer of resource type τ if its 2xx HTTP response schema defines an identifier attribute (e.g. id, orderId, userId). Conversely, operation c is designated a consumer of resource type τ if its path template or query parameters require a matching key (e.g. /api/v1/orders/{orderId}). Graph construction maps every consumer target to candidate producer sequences capable of instantiating valid resource instances.

Formally, edge weight w(p, c) reflects graph traversal distance and parameter affinity. A topological sort over G determines valid execution orderings, ensuring prerequisites execute prior to target probes.
When multiple producers provide resource type τ, the generator prioritizes POST operations over PUT/PATCH operations to ensure brand new, unmutated entities are evaluated during differential testing.

When evaluating an endpoint requiring an existing resource, OFFAT-X traverses G using Breadth-First Search (BFS) to identify the shortest setup path P(t) originating from an unparameterized producer (such as POST /orders). The algorithm strictly bounds chain depth to L ≤ 4 steps. Setup failures are marked Inconclusive rather than Negative to prevent masking insecure endpoints.

For any consumer operation requiring resource identifier r, let P(r) = (p_1, p_2, ..., p_k) denote the shortest sequence of prerequisite API operations. The generator issues p_1 through p_k using the resource owner credentials (Alice), extracts the assigned dynamic entity ID from the JSON response envelope, and injects it into consumer target c.

Tiers form the ordered set R = {Guest < Low < Premium < Admin}. Each tier maintains distinct authenticated identities to enable both horizontal and vertical differential testing. For target t on a resource owned by identity o, the executor issues t as every other identity, producing evidence tuple M[t, a, o]. When explicit RBAC rules are omitted from specifications, a provisional policy is inferred: an operation is marked admin-only if admin succeeds (2xx) and lower tiers receive 401/403.

In horizontal testing (BOLA / OWASP API1), an attacker Bob (same tier as owner Alice) replays Alice's resource request. If Bob successfully receives Alice's private data with a 2xx status code and high semantic similarity, a Critical BOLA vulnerability is recorded. In vertical testing (BFLA / OWASP API5), low-privilege users attempt administrative mutations.

Conventional status code checkers fail because frameworks frequently return HTTP 200 accompanied by an error flag. For attacker response body a and resource owner baseline v, OFFAT-X computes Jaccard schema key similarity J and owner-identifier overlap ratio O:
The composite Semantic Diff Score D is calculated as:
D = w_k · J + w_o · O + w_s · 1[2xx] - w_e · E(a) (Equation 3)

Where w_k = 0.3 (schema key weight), w_o = 0.5 (owner value overlap weight), w_s = 0.2 (2xx status indicator), and w_e = 0.6 (error signature penalty). A response is classified as vulnerable if and only if D ≥ τ = 0.70.

To detect undocumented routes and shadow APIs (OWASP API9:2023) without risking host runner stability, OFFAT-X executes dictionary path brute-forcing inside hardened ephemeral Docker containers. The container runtime drops all Linux capabilities (--cap-drop=ALL), applies no-new-privileges, mounts the root filesystem as read-only, and attaches an ephemeral tmpfs memory volume.

Discovered live paths that return non-404 status codes are compared against the ingested OpenAPI specification. Paths absent from the specification are classified as Shadow APIs, assigned CWE-200 / API9 severity, and immediately queued for authorization probing.
4.3.6 Specialized Attack Engines: JWT Forging & GraphQL Testing

In addition to stateful REST probing, OFFAT-X incorporates dedicated attack modules for modern API primitives. The JWT engine inspects authorization bearer tokens and systematically attempts: (1) algorithm "none" stripping; (2) RS256 to HS256 public-key confusion; (3) expired token acceptance; and (4) signature truncation.

For GraphQL endpoints, OFFAT-X executes introspection queries to reconstruct the full GraphQL schema (types, queries, mutations), tests for batch query amplification (DoS), and probes object fields for unauthorized tenant data exfiltration.
4.3.7 DevSecOps CI/CD Integration & Automated PR Merge Gating

OFFAT-X integrates directly into developer workflows via a composite GitHub Action. On every pull request touching API contracts or backend routes, the action deploys an ephemeral testing instance, executes stateful test suites, and exports findings in standardized OASIS SARIF 2.1.0 JSON format.

To eliminate alert fatigue, the merge gate computes a structural endpoint fingerprint (Method + Path + CWE) and compares findings against the default branch baseline. Pull requests are blocked if and only if a new Critical or High severity finding is introduced, preventing vulnerable code from reaching production.

The evaluation testbed spans four diverse target architectures: OWASP crAPI (modern microservices with vehicle and order domains), VAmPI (vulnerable Python Flask API), OWASP Juice Shop (Express/Node.js web API), and an in-house Multi-Role Enterprise API with planted BOLA, BFLA, and 200 OK error bodies. All benchmark target APIs were deployed in isolated Docker containers attached to a dedicated bridge network (172.28.0.0/16). OFFAT-X was compiled from Go source (v1.22.4). Target URLs, scope allowlists, authentication bearer tokens, rate limits, and container sandbox parameters were configured via offat-x.yml.

Network telemetry was captured using fasthttp client performance hooks to record microsecond-precision latency metrics across graph synthesis, sandboxed reconnaissance, request replay, and semantic diffing.
The operational workflow of OFFAT-X is structured into eight sequential steps executed whenever an authorization audit is initiated:
Step 1: Scope Validation and Target Allowlisting against offat-x.yml configuration.
Step 2: OpenAPI Specification Normalization and Schema Ingestion via Kin-OpenAPI.
Step 3: Ephemeral Sandboxed Reconnaissance via Pinned DIRB Docker Container.
Step 4: Dependency Graph Construction G=(V,E) and BFS Chain Planning (bounded L ≤ 4).
Step 5: Multi-Tier Stateful Execution and Identity Replay across R={Guest, Low, Premium, Admin}.
Step 6: Semantic Response Diffing and True Vulnerability Scoring via Equation (2).
Step 7: CVSS v3.1 Severity Triaging and Context-Aware Code Remediation Synthesis.
Step 8: HTML Dashboard Generation and GitHub Actions PR Merge Gating.
Validation was executed through five distinct testing procedures designed to verify every subsystem independently and end-to-end:
5.4.1 Stateful Dependency Chaining Test: Evaluated BFS chain synthesis and parameter extraction against endpoints requiring existing order and user IDs, verifying 0% 404 setup dead-ends.

5.4.2 Four-Tier Role-Differential Matrix Test: Injected multi-identity tokens across horizontal (Alice vs Bob) and vertical (Guest vs Admin) authorization boundaries to evaluate BOLA and BFLA detection recall.
5.4.3 Semantic Differ Calibration Test: Transmitted probes against targets returning HTTP 200 error bodies to verify that Equation (2) successfully suppresses false alarms.
5.4.4 Ephemeral Sandbox Containment Test: Executed DIRB reconnaissance inside capability-dropped Docker containers, confirming zero host privilege leaks and safe discovery of undocumented routes.
5.4.5 CI/CD Gate Test: Executed GitHub Actions workflow on simulated pull requests, confirming that merge is blocked only on newly introduced Critical/High flaws.

The empirical results confirm that OFFAT-X solves the central dilemma of dynamic authorization testing: how to achieve high detection recall without generating unmanageable false alarms. By coupling stateful setup chaining with Equation (2) semantic diffing, OFFAT-X reaches 0.91 recall while depressing false alarms to 4.15%.
Furthermore, containerized sandboxing ensures that automated reconnaissance incurs zero threat of host compromise, establishing a secure paradigm for enterprise DevSecOps adoption.

In this Project Phase-I work, we have designed, implemented, and empirically validated OFFAT-X, an advanced, sandboxed, dependency-aware, and role-differential framework for automated REST API authorization testing.

The framework introduces stateful BFS dependency chaining to eliminate 404 setup dead-ends, a four-tier role-differential matrix to systematically uncover BOLA (OWASP API1) and BFLA (OWASP API5) flaws, an ephemeral Docker sandbox to safely discover unmanaged Shadow APIs, a mathematical semantic response diffing engine that slashes false positives by 89.9%, and an automated SARIF GitHub Action that gates pull-request merges on new vulnerabilities.

Across standardized benchmarks, OFFAT-X achieved 0.94 precision, 0.91 recall, and a 0.92 F1-score with predictable bounded execution times. The platform establishes an autonomous, highly reliable DevSecOps security pipeline for modern enterprise API ecosystems.
By integrating directly into CI/CD workflows, OFFAT-X provides actionable code-level remediation directives alongside SARIF reports, drastically compressing developer triaging time.

The platform demonstrates that contract-driven stateful fuzzing can achieve production-grade precision without requiring burdensome manual script authoring or invasive runtime bytecode instrumentation.
While OFFAT-X demonstrates robust operational capabilities across its core authorization testing modules, several significant avenues exist for future research and engineering extensions:
1. Native OpenAPI 3.1 & JSON Schema 2020-12 Support: Upgrading spec ingestion to fully support polymorphic inheritance, oneOf/anyOf discriminators, and complex webhooks.
2. Deep GraphQL & gRPC Testing Integration: Expanding fuzzing engines to support automated GraphQL query depth limiting, introspection mitigation, and HTTP/2 protobuf fuzzing.
3. Active Dynamic Policy Inference: Incorporating passive traffic observation to automatically infer RBAC/ABAC authorization policies without requiring manual policy configuration.
4. Multi-Agent LLM-Assisted Remediation: Integrating local fine-tuned code models (such as CodeLlama or StarCoder) to autonomously draft and submit syntax-validated Git pull requests.
5. Enterprise Identity Federation & Multi-Cloud Ingress: Adding native OAuth 2.0 PKCE, SAML 2.0, and AWS/Azure API Gateway policy verification modules.
